title: The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference
summary: Viable Alternative of CUDA Moat, NVIDIA scared and working nights & weekends, Jensen’s Counter Submission, Kimi K3, Muse Spark Open, Qwen, GLM5.3, TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, Ray
story_key: story|title:the iron wood throne google s tpu stakes its claim on inference
content_excerpt: In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported. Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy . Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300. We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading. Previously, Jensen went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and commented on the fact that no other chips were taking advantage of their opportunity to show performance on InferenceX. Six months later, and indeed Google is taking full advantage of this opportunity. Today we are releasing the first official long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result: Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang). GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss. Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy. Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by

title: How Do AI Agents Waste Your Money?
summary: AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.

title: τ-bench-LILT: Evaluating Conversational Agents on Realistic Multilingual Tool-Use Tasks
summary: Frontier evaluations of tool-using conversational agents are conducted almost exclusively in English, leaving a critical gap for organizations deploying agents in other languages and regions. We present $τ$-bench-LILT, a multilingual extension of ${τ^3}$-bench covering German, Korean, Turkish, and Farsi in the airline, retail, telecom, and banking domains. We natively localize every layer of the benchmark: customer databases are populated with culturally appropriate records, user-simulator prompts are refined iteratively through contrastive annotation by native-language experts, and tasks are updated according to the localized database and to reflect realistic tasks in the target region. Evaluation across eight agent models shows the largest drops compared to English in the Korean and Farsi retail domains, by up to 61 points in pass^4. Code and data released at https://github.com/lilt/tau-bench-lilt.

title: Agents Are Going Async
summary: Async subagents let an agent stay responsive while background workers run long tasks. How the orchestrator, notifications and approvals work in Deep Agents.
story_key: story|title:agents are going async
content_excerpt: Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once. The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work. Claude Code runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's dots hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and DeepSeek Harness built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel. We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents . An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop. An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later. Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task , the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens: Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can report back on their own : A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting , and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. title: codex 0.167.0
summary:
New Features

  • Open the agent command center with codex agents --no-daemon. The command center and session picker now mark unread results (#58238, #58239, #58263, #58264).
  • Switch between connected backends from the terminal session picker and keep your drafts when switching (#58280, #58457).
  • Preview local image attachments while composing on supported terminals, and open viewed local images from clickable transcript paths (#58261, #58446).
  • Find API key and cloud provider options under “Sign in another way.” Enable gcp_setup_wizard to set up Google Cloud Vertex AI with Application Default Credentials or a credential file (#57857, #58427).
  • Opt into macOS or Windows system proxy settings from /experimental (#58157).
  • Expand patch details directly in the transcript while an approval prompt is open (#58281).

Bug Fixes

  • Saved chats stay visible after you switch model providers. If a chat can’t resume, you can read its transcript and prepare an editable prompt to continue in a new chat (#58202).
  • Ctrl+L clears the terminal display while keeping earlier messages available through Ctrl+T (#58266).
  • Deleting text that exposes a leading ! keeps an ordinary draft in chat mode (#58412).
  • Network approval prompts close when their requests end. Concurrent requests to the same endpoint prompt one at a time (#58350, #58351).
  • Long realtime V3 conversations save completed speech to chat history as the transcript grows (#58221).
  • Automatic context compaction now accounts for retained output from failed responses and responses with missing token usage data (#58404).

Documentation

  • The app-server README covers managed network constraints under [permissions.network] and prompt-user command rules that require fresh human approval (#58045, #58182).
  • The openai-docs skill recommends the documented replacement when migrating away from a deprecated model (#58134).

Chores

  • DotSlash manifests now reference the Cargo packages shipped with the release (#58717, #58757).
  • Linux musl builds use fewer allocator arenas to reduce idle memory after conversations unload (#58399).

title: Presentation Sensitivity in Typed Decision Models for Subjective Text Evaluation
summary: Typed decision models offer structured choices, scores, and probabilities for low-cost automated evaluation. We present a controlled audit of presentation sensitivity in Jev, Clef Flash, and Perplexity Decider across native choice and score interfaces. Across six datasets with 9,000 multiply annotated humor, helpfulness, and summarization items, we collect 702,000 judgments under interventions that vary positions, identifiers, authorship claims, endorsements, decision framing, and rating rubrics while preserving the evaluated texts. Jev's second-position probability advantage reaches 6.11 percentage points on summaries; reversing reader endorsements changes Perplexity's selected humor text on 40.40% of pairs; and rejection framing reduces Clef's summary agreement with human preferences by 23.36 points. Rating formats also shift score levels while often preserving rankings. Across these findings, repeatability, presentation robustness, and human alignment emerge as distinct properties of an evaluator. Reliable use therefore requires validating the decisions and score interpretations on which an evaluation pipeline depends.

title: LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
summary: LangSmith BYOC now runs on AWS (GA), Azure and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, and agent deployments stay in your cloud account while LangChain runs it.
story_key: story|title:langsmith byoc is now available on aws azure and google cloud
content_excerpt: LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) now runs on AWS (GA), Azure (Beta), and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates. By splitting the control plane and data plane in two, BYOC provides greater flexibily to decide where agents run and where telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith. LangChain runs the control plane , which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane , which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets. An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit. For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns. Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations. With BYOC, LangChain provisions and operates LangSmith inside your own virtual network. Consider a team running agent applications across several environments. With self-hosted, every update to the execution components meant coordinating downtime and managing custom Helm rollouts in each environment. With BYOC, the data in your data plane stays in your VPC while LangChain handles scaling, schema updates, and runtime dependencies. While self-hosting continues to be a reliable deployment option for customers who require complete control, BYOC provides the best of both worlds for customers who need it. Since we launched BYOC on AWS in August, many teams have chosen to run LangSmith in their own cloud with BYOC. They point to three main benefits: By expanding LangSmith BYOC to Azure and Google Cloud, more teams can get access to this experience while choosing their preferred cloud vendor. title: Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes
summary: Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.
story_key: model:vllm|title:introducing kinference an open source inference control plane for vllm and kuber
content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . title: ProcessPrefBench: Evaluating Cross-Task Transfer of Individual Process Preferences from Naturalistic Human-AI Interaction
summary: In natural human-AI dialogue, users' corrections, requests, and self-descriptions carry reusable signals about how they want work to be done. These signals reveal individual process preferences, user-specific standards for evidence, depth, analytical focus, procedure, and delivery. We ask whether a preference revealed in one dialogue can shape an assistant's later answer when the task does not restate it. ProcessPrefBench uses three months of natural dialogues from two knowledge workers to build 66 source-target cases separately judged for source evidence and target applicability. Sources are preselected, so the benchmark tests application rather than retrieval. We test three models with target-only, full-history, and distilled-preference prompts. Target-specific 0-2 rubrics score preference realization, and a task gate flags severe failures. Compared with target-only prompting, full-history and imperative distilled-preference prompting raise preference realization by 0.204 and 0.244 points on the 0-2 scale, respectively, with no reliable advantage from distillation. Fabricated-evidence failures rise from 5.8% under target-only prompting to 10.1% under full-history and 10.4% under imperative prompting. ProcessPrefBench highlights a tension in learning from dialogue, where drawing on prior interactions can improve preference realization yet also invite fabricated evidence. We hope it helps build assistants that honor a user's process preferences without sacrificing factual reliability.

title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
summary: Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.

title: From Delta Sharing to OpenSharing: what changed, what's next
summary: Delta Sharing has been the way thousands of organizations exchange live data across...
story_key: story|title:from delta sharing to opensharing what changed what s next
content_excerpt: How Delta Sharing became OpenSharing, an open, vendor-neutral protocol that extends zero-copy sharing beyond tables to agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data across platforms, and what the change means if you already share data today. Delta Sharing has been the way thousands of organizations exchange live data across clouds and platforms without copying it. In June 2026, Databricks and the Linux Foundation announced that Delta Sharing has evolved into OpenSharing , an open, vendor-neutral protocol for sharing not just tables, but the broader set of assets that AI teams now depend on: agent skills, AI models, and unstructured data. If you already share data with Delta Sharing, or you're evaluating how to collaborate with partners on both data and AI assets, this post walks through what OpenSharing actually is, what's changed under the hood, and where the project is headed. When Databricks introduced Delta Sharing at Data + AI Summit 2021, the core problem it addressed was simple to state and hard to solve well: organizations wanted to share live data with partners, customers, and other teams, without exporting files, standing up brittle ETL jobs, or forcing every recipient onto the same platform. Delta Sharing was contributed to the Linux Foundation as an open protocol, built on Delta Lake and Parquet, so a provider could grant access to a table and a recipient could query it directly, in real time, from tools like Apache Spark, Power BI, Tableau, pandas, and many others. That open, zero-copy model resonated. Delta Sharing grew into the most widely adopted open protocol for secure data sharing, used by organizations including Amadeus, Atlassian, LSEG, SAP, Stripe, and The Trade Desk for cross-cloud and cross-platform collaboration, according to Databricks ( Databricks press release ). By the time Databricks announced OpenSharing in June 2026, Delta Sharing had reached more than 28,000 data recipients, with roughly a third of shares flowing across platforms through open connectors rather than staying inside Databricks-to-Databricks sharing ( Databricks blog ). Sharing had already grown well beyond tables. Through Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, teams were exchanging views, volumes of unstructured files, notebooks, and registered ML models years before agents entered the picture, so structured data was never the whole story. What agents changed was the kind of asset that needed to move, and how far it needed to travel. Agent skills, the agents thems

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
